body_markdown:
Putting together something as complex as an automobile can be intimidating for many, and it’s hard to blame them. There are so many parts and pieces, and it’s not always immediately clear which bits are the critical linchpin in a system and which are perfectly acceptable to use in a “good enough” condition. While this often leads me down the very dangerous “while I’m in there” rabbit hole of financial ruin that keeps the car on jack stands an extra month or two, sometimes it leads to a better understanding of the systems that makes it all worth the time and money. Other times it shows just how little can be needed to ensure safe operation.


I’ve been chipping away at sorting out my LS-swapped Corvette, and the process has introduced me to new problems with surprisingly simple solutions. Or, put another way, simple projects that allow me to focus on the bigger “problems.” The whole project has been phased in a way that the drivetrain is getting ironed out before the rest of the chassis gets the same attention. That meant driving quite a few miles and—at least at first—just crossing my fingers and hoping for the best. Luckily, I stacked the deck in my favor with just a few simple and affordable parts to ensure that the things that were likely to break wouldn’t take out other parts of the car or me with it. I can deal with being stranded, but I don’t enjoy being damaged. Here’s what helped.


## Stainless steel braided brake lines


Sure, this means I need to re-bleed the brake system, but that never hurts on an old car.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Totally refreshed? Hardly. But safe.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


The stainless lines are direct fit and replacement is fairly painless since this Corvette is not rusty.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Trusting your brakes is a critical part of driving any car, but when I shoved way too much power under the giant clamshell hood of this Corvette, I realized the key to reining all those galloping ponies in was all flowing through 41-year-old rubber lines that connected the hard brake lines to the calipers. These lines are critical to allowing the suspension to do its thing but also keep the brakes functioning.


Rubber lines often look totally fine at arm’s length, but when you start thinking about the dynamics of how those hoses age, replacing them early and often becomes an item that should land on every project car to-do list. The hoses on my ‘Vette had a small amount of cracking, but only after pulling them off did I see that a lot of the swelling of the rubber was working to close the internal passage of the hose rather than expand the outer diameter. Brakes that work are critical to a safe car, and I shouldn’t have waited as long as I did to replace these. At $150, they weren’t cheap, but I sleep better at night knowing the stainless braided lines are not going to have this issue.


## Holley Bluetooth dongle


This dash will work again, but it’s going to take a minute.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


While not perfect, this gauge cluster works and is customizable.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Knowledge is power, and that includes knowing the critical information about how the engine is running. The digital dash on this Corvette is a feature I have every intention of fixing. I am planning to ensure it works in a factory manner despite the engine swap. Since the dash is divorced from the factory engine control computer, this shouldn’t take much more than an adapter box for the speedometer that can convert the speed signal from the sensor in the Tremec T56 into one that will light up the right pixels on the dash. Same for the tachometer, oil pressure, temperature, and charging voltage.


But doing all that takes time, and I want to drive at least a little—okay, a lot—between now and when I get the dash working. Luckily, I can cheat a bit and use the new Holly Performance ECU to tell me a lot of the information I wanted to know. But instead of a nice large dash display, I get to look at an old phone that I wasn’t going to get trade-in money for last time I upgraded. Via a Bluetooth connection directly to the ECU, this old phone could show me all the information from the engine’s sensors as well as GPS speed thanks to the internal GPS on the phone. Directly in front of me: dead gauges. Just to the right in the center of the dash: Just about all the information I could ask for, with the additional benefit of being able to do plenty of tuning changes as well—all for[just over $200](https://www.holley.com/products/fuel_systems/fuel_injection/terminator_x/terminator_x_and_x_max_ford_kits/parts/558-483) .


## New U-joint straps and hardware


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


When talking about drivetrains and engine swaps, there are a lot of small parts that fall through the cracks of conversation. It’s often unintentional, as there are just so many items to keep track of and at some point we have to say “good enough.” The only problem is drawing the line in the sand without understanding the consequences of inaction in some critical areas.


In my case, this was the U-joint hardware. Replacing the U-joints was a definite, but on any previous car I’ve gone through, the bolts and straps that hold the U-joint in place on the driveshaft, hub, or slip yoke were items that got reused without a second thought. The 1965 Corvair that occasionally gets parked next to this Corvette in the garage is the prime example. It got new U-joints a while back, but the hardware was in good enough shape. Well, that Corvair makes one-quarter the horsepower of this Corvette, and likely even less torque, and gets driven in a completely different manner.


Losing a driveshaft on the Corvette would be a very bad day, and once I saw that new hardware to hold the U-joints in place on the hubs and drive flanges was under $80 to replace *everything,* it became a no-brainer. I’m replacing so much that this really isn’t even a “while I’m in there” but rather just common sense.


All three of these items allowed me to drive and start sorting out this project in a way that I feel safe. Things may fail, but catastrophic failure is now much less likely. I’ve got too much money tied up so far to risk stepping backwards. Now I can continue forward with minimal distraction. What a luxury.
